extracted.intended_audience: researchers, comedians, joke-writers, and anyone interested in empirical findings about humor and joke design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for crafting short jokes aimed at broad audiences based on LaughLab's large-scale empirical study of joke funniness across cultures and demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke make someone feel superior to a target?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of three elements commonly present in the funniest jokes — the audience feels smarter or elevated relative to a character or target in the joke. This can be achieved by depicting another person or group as inept, foolish, or less knowledgeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected twist / incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it have an unexpected twist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor strongly correlates with incongruity and surprise — an unexpected response or reversal is a core ingredient. Structure the joke so the punchline violates the audience's prediction in a concise way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch of darkness / mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it touch on darkness or mortality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many top-rated jokes include a 'sad feeling of mortality' or a dark element (e.g., death). A gentle or clever dark undertone can increase perceived funniness, but cultural/audience sensitivity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate ideal length (~100 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke roughly 100 words long?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab found jokes containing about 103 words rated highest (the winning joke was 102 words). This suggests a sweet spot: longer than a one-liner/soundbite but shorter than an essay — enough setup to build expectation before the twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match cultural preferences of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke match the cultural humor preference of the target audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different national/regional groups prefer different joke types. Tailor content to the audience's taste rather than assuming a one-size-fits-all joke will work across cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural style preferences (regional patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which style of humor does the target culture prefer (examples from LaughLab)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the study: British/Irish/NZ/Australian audiences preferred wordplay/puns; French/Danish/Belgian preferred surreal humor; American/Canadian favored superiority themes (one group's superiority over another); Germans found a wide range of jokes funny. Use these patterns when localizing jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content cues: animal choice (ducks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke use animals or specific content correlated with funniness (e.g., ducks)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found animal jokes with ducks rated funnier than other animals. This is an empirical association — useful for idea generation but not a guarantee of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic features: hard consonants (esp. 'K')
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke employ phonetic features associated with funniness, such as hard consonants?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab noted a correlation between funniness and hard consonant sounds (particularly the 'K' sound). Consider phonetic punchiness when writing lines intended to land sharply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/contextual factors (time-of-day effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the timing/context of presentation aligned with times when jokes are rated funnier?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study observed a peak funniness time (Wednesday afternoon at ~6:03pm). Timing of presentation/testing/distribution can affect ratings — consider audience context when collecting responses or scheduling posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical rating method: 5-point funniness scale
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab used a 5-point scale from 'not very funny' to 'very funny' with 350,000 raters. When evaluating jokes empirically, use a simple ordinal scale and gather demographic data to analyze subgroup differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic tracking and audience segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Were demographics (sex, age, nationality) recorded and used to analyze funniness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting demographic data allowed the study to identify cross-cultural and age/sex patterns. For targeted humor, segment responses by audience demographics to tune material.
